clinicalPearls: Symmetrical ash-grey to blue-grey macules and patches, mainly over the trunk, proximal limbs and neck
Early active lesions may show a slightly raised erythematous border that later resolves, leaving grey pigmentation
Considered by many authors to lie within the spectrum of lichen planus pigmentosus
The grey colour reflects dermal melanin held within melanophages, the result of an interface reaction with pigment incontinence
Wood-lamp does not accentuate the dermal pigment, and biopsy helps confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimics
The course is chronic and often resistant to treatment, so drugs, contactants and other triggers should be sought and removed
More commonly reported in younger patients and in those with darker skin
reference.pathophysiology: A lichenoid interface dermatitis damages the basal layer of the epidermis, causing pigment incontinence in which melanin escapes into the papillary dermis. There it is taken up by melanophages, and the deep location of this melanin gives the characteristic ashy-grey hue. The trigger is usually idiopathic, though drugs, chemicals and infections have been implicated in some cases.
additionalDifferentials: Fixed drug eruption or other drug-induced pigmentation
Diffuse pigmentation of Addison disease or haemochromatosis
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy to confirm the interface pattern with dermal melanophages
Wood-lamp examination confirming non-accentuated dermal pigment
Targeted screening for systemic or infective mimics when the picture is atypical
redFlags: Features of systemic disease such as Addisonian pigmentation with weight loss and fatigue
A temporal link to a new drug suggesting a drug-induced eruption
Endemic exposure raising the possibility of pinta or another treponematosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but chronic and persistent; it may fade slowly over years, with a better tendency to resolve in children than in adults.
pitfalls: Expecting a response to topical lightening agents against dermal pigment
Overlooking systemic mimics of diffuse hyperpigmentation
Failing to distinguish it from lichen planus pigmentosus or post-inflammatory change
management: Identification and removal of potential triggers, including causative drugs, contactants and any underlying infection
A trial of topical calcineurin inhibitors or topical corticosteroids on active inflammatory (bordered) lesions, recognising that established grey pigment responds poorly
Consideration of dapsone or narrowband ultraviolet phototherapy in extensive or progressive disease, given the limited and inconsistent evidence
Photoprotection to limit further darkening of the dermal pigment
Reassurance about the benign nature, with cosmetic camouflage for cosmetically troublesome pigmentation
Confirmatory skin biopsy and dermatological follow-up to exclude mimics and monitor a chronic, often treatment-resistant course
